title: Sample Lottery: Unsupervised Discovery of Critical Instances for LLM Reasoning
claim: Conventional approaches annotate everything and spend compute uniformly; ours selects a few critical samples, annotating and training on them for comparable performance.
layout: 2 stacked rows, left-to-right flows, double arrow linking outcomes on right
description: Two horizontal flows are stacked to contrast conventional training with the proposed paradigm. A stack of paper cards on the far left shows an unlabeled math question (a recurrence sequence) as the shared starting point. Top row (a), Conventional Approaches: a big arrow leads to a tired cartoon annotator with a pile of papers, labeled 'Tedious Annotation Over the Entire Dataset'. Next is a purple box of many question and answer cards with several GPUs, labeled 'Uniform Allocation of Resources', then an arrow to a robot labeled Optimization. Bottom row (b), The Proposed Paradigm: the dataset passes through a red box, 'Complementary Conformal Selection', to a small subset. A relaxed annotator is labeled 'Minimal Annotation Effort'. A green box shows few cards and one GPU, labeled 'Concentrated Computation', then a robot. A double-headed arrow between the two robots reads 'Comparable Performance'. The sketchy hand-drawn style uses pastel colors.
caption: Conventional approaches require tedious full annotation over the entire dataset and allocate computation resources uniformly across the training set. By comparison, this work selects lotterywinning samples from the training set in an unsupervised manner, and then optimizes the model using these critical instances only, achieving comparable performance.
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR) has equipped large language models (LLMs) with the capability of reasoning over complicated logical problems through policy optimization. However, conventional methods require complete annotation of the entire dataset and allocate computation uniformly over all samples. We articulate the lottery sample hypothesis in policy optimization of LLMs: a large training set contains a small subset that, when trained alone, yields performance comparable to that of the full dataset. This paper therefore explores the following question: How can we identify these lottery-winning samples from the original dataset without access to answers? Unlike prior efforts that analyze the effect of different samples in the training set with complete annotation, this paper focuses on the unsupervised discovery of critical instances for LLM reasoning and proposes a novel framework termed Complementary Conformal Selection (CONST). Specifically, CONST evaluates the importance of samples by considering two complementary components: procedural volatility and outcome volatility. Procedural volatility measures the potential variations during the LLM’s reasoning process, while outcome volatility captures inconsistencies in the final answer. Subsequently, conformal prediction is used to obtain a prediction set whose cardinality serves as the criterion for selecting the lottery-winning samples for annotation. We also provide a theoretical analysis, showing that CONST can effectively approximate the optimal policy. Extensive experiments on various LLMs across different datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of CONST.
